source_evidence.finding: IAU recognizes 88 constellations with three-letter Latin abbreviations, defines them as bounded sky areas, and says their line patterns are not formal definitions; it also explains that apparent stellar groupings usually are not physically connected.
ESO identifies M87 as a large elliptical galaxy about 55 million light-years away in Virgo and identifies its central object as a supermassive black hole.

The dated 10 April 2019 release reports the first direct visual evidence of the M87 black hole and its shadow; it gives 55 million light-years and 6.5 billion solar masses, eight ground-based radio telescopes, an Earth-sized virtual telescope, a ring-like structure with a dark central shadow, and the gravitational-bending/capture interpretation.

articles.factual_and_pedagogical_assessment: The article accurately separates Virgo as a formal sky region, M87 as a galaxy in that direction, and M87's central black hole. The numerical values, date, array description, and careful non-surface explanation match the opened ESO material; the self-check reinforces the intended scale distinction.

source_evidence.finding: IAU's formal-area definition, 88-constellation list, and convention-versus-physical-connection distinction support Ophiuchus/Oph as a map reference rather than a physically bound star group.

NASA's 12 July 2023 first-anniversary release gives 390 light-years, about 50 young solar-mass-or-smaller stars, dense dust around protostars, red bipolar molecular-hydrogen jets, S1 as the only substantially more massive star, and disk shadows described as potential future planetary systems.

ESA/Webb identifies the Rho Ophiuchi cloud complex as a 390-light-year object in Ophiuchus; it specifies infrared filters, says young-star jets light molecular hydrogen shown red, and describes circumstellar-disk shadows as future planetary-system material.

articles.factual_and_pedagogical_assessment: The article accurately distinguishes the Ophiuchus sky region, the Rho Ophiuchi cloud complex, and a disk around an individual young star. The wording correctly retains uncertainty about planets in a disk and matches the opened NASA and ESA/Webb descriptions.
